dients, since apart from its skin-whitening properties, it adds brightness to the skin, prevents the formation of wrinkles and has important antioxidative properties, thus it is considered as antiaging agent [7, 8].

However, the use of AA in cosmetic products has been limited owing to its labile oxidative properties, which can be accelerated in the presence of oxygen, water, light, heat and metals $[9–11]$ . In order to avoid its early degradation, different derivatives have been designed, such as ascorbyl phosphate (APH; as magnesium or sodium salts) and ascorbyl palmitate (AP), and more recently ascorbyl glucoside (AG). As can be seen from their molecular structures shown in Fig. 1, the enediol moiety, responsible for AA oxidation, is blocked in case of APH and AG, leading to higher stability than AP. All these derivatives are hydrolysed by the skin cells, which cause the in situ liberation of the AA $[12, 13]$ .

No substantive dermatological problems associated to the use of skin-whitening cosmetics containing AA and its derivates have been reported $[14]$ ; however, their determination in cosmetic products is necessary in order to control the efficacy of such products. Despite this, no official analytical methods have been published to control them. Moreover, unfortunately, there are only few papers reporting the determination of AA and/or some of its derivatives in skin-whitening products, as recently reviewed by Chisvert et al. $[6]$ . LC with UV/visible spectrometry (UV/Vis) detection is the technique of choice in determining AA $[15, 16]$ , AG $[17, 18]$ , AP $[19]$ and APH $[15, 17, 19–23]$ . Octadecylsilica ( $C_{18}$ ) columns are the most popular columns employed, although the use of amipropyl $[20]$ or cyanopropyl $[19]$ bonded silica columns are proposed by some authors to carry out the retention and subsequent determination of the most ionic analyte (i.e. APH). Another strategy to retain and determine ionic analytes, using $C_{18}$ columns, is the use of mobile phase modifiers that make the retention of AA $[15]$ and APH $[21, 23]$ possible by ion-pairs formation.
On the other hand, in a recently published paper, the simultaneous determination of AA, APH and AP is carried out by micellar electrokinetic CE [24].
Three other papers, proposing voltammetry for the individual determination of APH [25] and AG [26], and for the simultaneous determination of AA, AP and APH [27] can be found in the literature.

However, most of these methods employ non-environmentally friendly organic solvents. Moreover, taking into account that these four skin-whitening agents can usually be mixed in cosmetic products, there is need for a wide-ranging method able to determine AA together with all its derivatives currently used in skin-whitening cosmetics.

Thus, the aim of this paper focuses on developing an analytical method able to determine the four above-mentioned compounds in cosmetic products. The method is based on the use of LC-UV/Vis, using environmentally friendly solvents in every step of the analytical procedure.

A Jasco LC system equipped with a Jasco PU-2089 Plus high-pressure pump and a Jasco MD-2010 Plus diode array detector (DAD; Tokyo, Japan) was employed. Performing the experiment in triplicate (three times) is a standard statistical practice to account for experimental error and ensure the reliability of the final results. The use of deionized water is important because it lacks the ions and impurities found in tap water, which could otherwise interfere with the chemical reactions or detection methods used later.

Sonication involves using high-frequency sound waves to create cavitation bubbles in the liquid. When these bubbles collapse, they generate intense local energy that helps to break down cell walls or aggregates, thereby enhancing the extraction of the target compounds (AA and APH) into the solution. This ensures that the concentration measured in the liquid phase accurately reflects the total amount present in the original sample.

3.1 Preliminary study of the solvent for sample preparation

Although the four target analytes belong to the same chemical family, they display different physico-chemical behaviour due to the different chemical moieties of their molecular structures. On one hand, AA, APH and AG are water-soluble chemicals, whereas on the other hand, AP is a fat-soluble chemical. Given the different solubility
properties of these four target analytes, a study of the solvent was necessary. As expected, high EtOH content made AA, APH and AG solubility difficult, whereas AP solubility became easier. Moreover, high EtOH content helps to solve other components from sample, thus making analyte lixiviation easier. An optimal EtOH content of 65% was used to solve all four target analytes, and moreover, it was enough to lixiviate the analytes from samples.

First of all, the study was focused to exclude AP, since it is the most fat-soluble target analyte, thus it eluted later than the others. In this first step, a solution of 50 $\mu$ g/mL of the other three target analytes in EtOH/50 mM phosphate buffer at the same pH as the mobile phase (65:35, v/v) was injected using different mobile phases (at 1 mL/min) constituted by 100% 50 mM phosphate buffer at a pH ranging from 2 to 6. As can be seen in Fig. 2, the best resolution was achieved at pH 3, where although AA was resolved from AG and APH, these last compounds overlapped.

In order to achieve a better resolution of the peaks, the effect of the flow rate was studied over the range of 0.5–1.5 mL/min (results not shown), by injecting a solution of 50 $\mu$ g/mL of the target analytes into EtOH/50 mM phosphate buffer pH 3 (65:35, v/v). To fully appreciate the data presented in the table above, let us break down what these metrics tell us about the performance of this chromatographic method. Think of this table as the "report card" for our analytical tool. Each column represents a different aspect of the method's reliability and sensitivity.

**Retention Time** is the time it takes for a specific compound to travel through the column and reach the detector. The values listed (e.g., 5.19 min for APH) are the average times, with the $\pm$ value indicating the standard deviation. A small standard deviation (like $\pm 0.02$) is excellent news; it means the method is highly reproducible. If you run the same sample multiple times, the compound will appear at almost exactly the same moment every time, much like a clock that keeps perfect time.

**RSD in area** (Relative Standard Deviation) measures the precision of the detector's response. An RSD of 0.4% to 0.7% is remarkably low. In practical terms, this means that if you measure the "size" (area) of the peak for a given concentration, the variation between repeated measurements is less than 1%. This high precision ensures that small differences in concentration won't be lost in the noise of the measurement.

**Dynamic range** indicates the span of concentrations over which the method can accurately quantify the analyte. The values here (e.g., <215 μg/mL for APH) suggest the method is robust across a wide variety of sample concentrations, from trace amounts up to higher levels, without needing to dilute or concentrate the sample significantly.

**Intercept and Slope** are parameters from the calibration curve, which is the mathematical relationship between the detector signal (peak area) and the known concentration of the analyte.
*   The **Slope** represents the sensitivity of the method. A higher slope means the detector produces a larger signal for a given amount of analyte. For instance, AA has a slope of $2150 \pm 30$, which is significantly higher than AP's slope of $517 \pm 2$. This tells us that the detector is much more sensitive to AA than to AP under these conditions.
*   The **Intercept** ideally should be zero (meaning no signal when no analyte is present). The values here are small and close to zero, which is good, though the uncertainty (e.g., $\pm 20$ for AA) is relatively large compared to the slope, suggesting some baseline noise or minor systematic error, but it is acceptable for quantitative work.

**$R^2$ (Coefficient of Determination)** tells us how well the data points fit the linear calibration curve. Values of 0.9994 to 0.99997 are extremely close to 1.0, indicating an almost perfect linear relationship between concentration and signal. This linearity is crucial for accurate quantification across the entire dynamic range.

**LOD (Limit of Detection)** is the lowest concentration of an analyte that can be reliably distinguished from background noise. The LODs range from 2 to 6 μg/mL. This means the method is sensitive enough to detect these compounds even at very low levels, which is essential for analyzing trace impurities or low-concentration ingredients in complex matrices.

The data in Table 3 demonstrates that the proposed method is precise, sensitive, and linear for all four analytes. This sets the stage for the next critical step: validating the method against established reference techniques to ensure that the results are not just precise, but also accurate.

It is worth mentioning that the proposed method enables the determination of AA in all the samples, whereas this analyte was overlapped with matrix compounds when the reference method was employed.

This is a significant practical advantage of the new method. In analytical chemistry, "matrix effects" or "overlap" occur when other components in the sample (the matrix) produce signals at the same time or wavelength as the target analyte, making it impossible to measure the analyte accurately. The fact that the reference method suffered from this overlap for AA, while the proposed LC-UV method did not, highlights the superior selectivity of the new approach. It allows for the clean, unambiguous quantification of AA even in complex samples where older methods fail.

Let's examine the validation results for a real-world application: a skin-whitening sample. This table compares the "Real content" (the known amount added to the sample, acting as the ground truth) with the "Found content" (the amount measured by our new method).

The **Error (%)** column is the key metric here. It is calculated as $\frac{\text{Found} - \text{Real}}{\text{Real}} \times 100$.
*   For **APH**, the error is -0.8%. This is exceptionally low, indicating high accuracy.
*   For **AG**, the error is -4.2%. While slightly higher, this is still generally considered acceptable in many pharmaceutical and cosmetic analyses, especially given the complexity of the matrix.
*   For **AA**, the error is -1.4%, again showing good accuracy.
*   For **AP**, the error is -3.1%.

The small standard deviations ($s$) in the "Found content" column (e.g., $\pm 0.002$) reinforce the precision we saw in Table 3. The fact that the errors are consistently negative but small suggests a very slight, consistent underestimation, but nothing that would compromise the validity of the results. This table proves that the method works not just in ideal laboratory conditions, but in a complex, real-world product.
On the other hand, as can be seen in the results obtained by the proposed method, the RSD values were in the 1.2–5.7% range, which are similar to those obtained employing other methods.

This statement provides context for the precision of the method when applied to actual samples (as opposed to the pure standards in Table 3). The RSD (Relative Standard Deviation) for the sample analysis is slightly higher (1.2–5.7%) than for the pure standards (0.4–0.7%), which is expected. Real samples are more complex, leading to slightly more variability. However, the key point is that these values are "similar to those obtained employing other methods." This means our new method is no less precise than the established reference methods, confirming its reliability for routine analysis.

In order to evaluate the accuracy of the results obtained by the proposed method, the results obtained for all the analytes and samples were compared with those obtained by the reference methods, by means of a linear regression model. The obtained equation was: $Y = (0.995 \pm 0.005)X - (0.008 \pm 0.006)$ , $R^{2} = 0.99991$ , N = 8, where Y and X are expressed in % w/w of each analyte and are the results obtained by the proposed method and the results taken as reference, respectively. The theoretical t-value for a 5% significance level and N-2 degrees of freedom is 2.45, and the experimental t-values for the slope and the intercept were 1.07 and 1.27, respectively, which shows the comparability of the results.

This is the most rigorous statistical proof of the method's validity. We are comparing the results from our new method ($Y$) against the results from the trusted reference method ($X$). If the two methods are equivalent, the data points should fall on a line with a slope of 1 and an intercept of 0.

Let's deconstruct the regression equation: $Y = (0.995 \pm 0.005)X - (0.008 \pm 0.006)$.

1.  **The Slope ($0.995 \pm 0.005$):** The ideal slope is 1.0. Our experimental slope is 0.995, which is extremely close to 1. The uncertainty ($\pm 0.005$) means the true slope lies between 0.990 and 1.000. Since 1.0 is within this range, we can statistically conclude that the slope is not significantly different from 1. This means there is no proportional bias; if the reference method says the concentration is 10%, our method says it's 9.95%, which is essentially the same.
2.  **The Intercept ($-0.008 \pm 0.006$):** The ideal intercept is 0. Our experimental intercept is -0.008. The uncertainty is $\pm 0.006$, meaning the true intercept lies between -0.014 and -0.002. Since 0 is *not* strictly within this narrow range (it's just outside), there might be a tiny constant bias. However, let's look at the t-test to be sure.
3.  **The $R^2$ value ($0.99991$):** This indicates an almost perfect linear correlation between the two methods. The data points from the new method track the reference method's results very closely.
4.  **The t-test:** This is the formal statistical test to determine if the slope and intercept are significantly different from their ideal values (1 and 0, respectively).
    *   We compare the **experimental t-value** to the **theoretical t-value** (critical value) at a 5% significance level.
    *   Theoretical t-value = 2.45.
    *   Experimental t-value for the slope = 1.07. Since $1.07 < 2.45$, the slope is **not** significantly different from 1.
    *   Experimental t-value for the intercept = 1.27. Since $1.27 < 2.45$, the intercept is **not** significantly different from 0.

**Conclusion from the t-test:** Because both experimental t-values are smaller than the theoretical critical value, we fail to reject the null hypothesis that the slope is 1 and the intercept is 0. In plain English: **The proposed method is statistically comparable to the reference method.** There is no significant bias, either proportional or constant. This is a gold-standard validation.

In the case of AG (contained in sample A), for which no reference method was applied, recovery was obtained using the proposed method by means of the standard calibration approach, showing a value statistically comparable to 100% for this analyte in sample A, which shows the absence of proportional error caused by the matrix of the sample.

For one of the analytes, AG, we couldn't use the reference method comparison because no reference method existed for it in this specific sample. So, how do we prove accuracy? We use a **recovery study**.

In a recovery study, we add a known amount of the analyte (AG) to a sample and then measure how much we find. If we add 10% and find 10%, the recovery is 100%. If we find 95%, the recovery is 95%, suggesting a 5% loss or bias. The text states that the recovery was "statistically comparable to 100%." This means that, within the limits of experimental error, we recovered exactly what we added. This is crucial because it proves that the complex matrix of the skin-whitening cream did not interfere with the measurement of AG. There is no "proportional error" caused by the matrix, confirming that the method is robust and accurate even without a direct reference comparison.
